the 4-chloophenol-degradating strain A. chlorophenicus was able to colonize and grow in soil contaminated with its substrate.

the bacterial community structure in soil is impacted by the presence of a biodegradation substrate, and by inoculation of a biodegrading bacterial strain into the soil, as determined by T-RFLT analysis.

the impact of 3 different stress factors on the soil bacterial community and the resulting changes in bacterial community structure.

the development of a molecular tool that will enable the monitoring of a biodegrading bacterial inoculum in soil, the identification of the bacterial community structure, and the assessment of the impact of biodegrading bacterial strains on the indigenous bacterial community.

the impact of 2 stress scenarios, 4-chloropnenol and inoculation with the biodegrader, on bacterial community structure in soil and the potential of T-RFLP as a tool for assessing the impact of these stress scenarios.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the 4-chloophenol-degradative strain Arthrobacter chlorophenolicus A6 (chromosomaly tagged with luc) was inoculate into 4-chlorophonl-contaminated soil and the impact of this bioaugmentation on the indigenous microbiotia was assessed.

the 4-chlorophenol-degrading A. chlorophenicus A6L was able to survive and proliferate in a 4-chloropnenol-contaminated microcosm, and was able to degrade a significant portion of the added 4-chloropheol.
the bacterial community in the soil was significantly altered by the presence of 4-chloophenol and by inoculation with A6L.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the soil microbiota is a highly dynamic and responsive community that can be significantly altered by the presence or absence of a biodegrading inoculum and/or a specific pollutant.
the soil microbiota can respond to specific stress scenarios in a rapid and dynamic fashion, and that this may have implications for the bioremediation potential of the soil microbiota.
bioaugmentation may be a viable approach to enhance degradation of recalcitrant compounds in soil.
